ticket.title: task_updated writes the event log but never refreshes the ticket projection, so 8 of 166 root tickets serve a description their projection does not hold
ticket.description: A ticket file is a projection plus an event log, and the projection is supposed to be the materialised current state. It is written when the ticket is created and NOT refreshed by task_updated: `storypole update --desc` / `--append-desc` append an event and leave the projection as it was. Measured 2026-11-10 on the root store: 8 of 166 tickets serve a description that differs from their projection, 6 of them with an entirely empty projection because the description arrived after creation (the defer-then-update flow GB-347 itself went through). Readers disagree as a result: `storypole show` replays and shows the real text, while anything that reads the JSON projection - including `remint` dry run citation counts and any script - sees the stale or empty one. `update` should write the projection it just changed, or the store should expose one rebuild that guarantees projection == replay. Found while proving GB-347: it is why remint citation rewrites landed on a field nothing serves.

CORRECTED AND FIXED 2026-11-10 — the premise of this ticket was wrong; the reader was the bug.

WHAT I CLAIMED. That a ticket file's projection "is supposed to be the materialised current state" and that `task_updated`
failing to refresh it was the defect. That is not what the store says it is.

WHAT IS TRUE. `TicketRecord.ticket` is documented as "the task as CREATED; later events carry every change", and the code
agrees: almost nothing reads it for state. Across storypole-core, storypole-cli and storypole-mcp the only reads of
`record.ticket` are `.id` (identity, which no rename touches) and `.ticket_key` (the file's name). Every read of current
state goes through `replay()`. So 8 of 166 tickets differing from their projection is the design working, not drift.

THE ACTUAL DEFECT, which the same measurement found. `remint` counted a ticket's citations against the projection:
  `remint_cmds::read_refs` read `ticket.description` and `ticket.edges` straight out of the file.
A description set after creation lives only in the events, so the dry run under-reported the work it was about to do -
and on the common fixture it under-reported a 39-citation rewrite as 9. Fixed: `read_refs` now deserialises the record and
uses `replay()` for the description and the edge list, falling back to the projection only when a record cannot replay.
Test: `citations_are_counted_from_replay_not_from_the_creation_snapshot`.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PROJECTION, and why nothing else changed. A projection that is deliberately a creation snapshot
needs one thing the store lacked: a reader that knows it. The field is documented, the readers now agree, and the
`projection != replay` counts measured during `GB-347` (common 5, benchwork 2, storypole 4 uuids) are expected values of
that design rather than damage. No write path was changed and no projection was rewritten: refreshing every projection
would duplicate the log into the file it already sits beside, and every consumer would still have to know which copy wins.

The lesson worth keeping: "the log is the source of truth" was learned twice this session - once when a remint rewrote
only the projection (`GB-347`), and once when a count read only the projection. Both are the same mistake seen from
opposite ends.

REPRODUCED 2026-11-10, and the write that goes stale is not only task_updated. After storypole verify SP-49 succeeded, the ticket file storypole/.gaugeblock/storypole/tickets/SP-49.json held a ticket block reading status triage with verification_receipt null, while its own events array already carried the task_verified event and storypole show answered Verified with a full receipt. So the projection and the record in the same file disagreed, and ledger-reconcile agreed with the events rather than the snapshot - verified 1 versus 1, index and ledger agree. The consequence is a reader that trusts the ticket block: replay recovers the truth, so nothing is lost, but anything reading the block directly serves the pre-verify state until some later write happens to rewrite it. Worth widening this ticket from task_updated to every event whose projection lives in the ticket block, with verify as the second measured instance.

MEASURED AGAIN 2026-11-10, and the gap has grown: reading the ticket JSON directly reports 148 active tickets while the store reports 77, so 71 ticket blocks are stale - archived in the event log and still carrying a live status in their own projection. SP-36, SP-37 and SP-40 are three of them: verified and archived today, still reading in_progress in their files. The same read also miscounts plans, which is how a plan inventory taken from the files would conclude 4 tickets have plans when the store says 3. Priority raised: every tool that reads records rather than replaying them gets a wrong answer, and this session produced two separate reports from that mistake (a board count and a plan audit).
